Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 95, verse 1–3:

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿By the fig and the olive, (1) And Mount Sinai, (2) And this secure city.﴾ [At-Tin 1-3] to the end of the surah.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿By the fig and the olive, (1) And Mount Sinai, (2) And this secure city﴾ is an oath by these four things. Allah swore by the fig, the olive, Mount Sinai, and this secure city, meaning Makkah, because the surah is Meccan, so the one referred to ("this") is near, and it is Makkah. The tin (fig) is the well-known fruit, and likewise the zaytun (olive). Allah swore by them because they are abundant in Palestine.

﴿And Mount Sinai﴾: Allah swore by it because it is the mountain at which Allah spoke to Musa (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family).

﴿And this secure city﴾: Allah swore by it, meaning Makkah, because it is the most beloved of the lands to Allah and the most noble of the lands in the sight of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Some scholars said: Allah swore by these three because the first, ﴿the fig and the olive﴾, is the land of Palestine in which the prophets were, and the last of the prophets of the Children of Israel is 'Isa ibn Maryam (peace be upon him). And Mount Sinai, because it is the mountain around which Allah, exalted is He, revealed to Musa. As for the secure city, it is Makkah, from which Allah sent Muhammad (ﷺ).

The scholars said: The meaning of His saying ﴿And Mount Sinai﴾ is: the mountain of blessing, because Allah, exalted is He, described it, or described what is around it, as the sacred valley.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 95, verses 4–5:**

﴿Indeed, We created man in the best of stature.﴾ [At-Tin: 4] This is the matter sworn to. Allah, exalted is He, swore that He created man in the best of stature. If you reflect upon the sentence, that is, the sentence containing the matter sworn to, it becomes clear that it is emphasized with three emphasizers: the oath, the lam (of emphasis), and *qad*. So Allah swore that He created man in the best of stature: in the best of stature in form and creation, and in the best of stature in disposition (fitrah) and purpose. This is because there is no creature whose creation is better than that of the children of Adam. All the earthly creatures are below the children of Adam in creation, for Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, We created man in the best of stature.﴾

﴿Then We returned him to the lowest of the low.﴾ [At-Tin: 5] This return that Allah, mighty and majestic, mentions means that Allah, exalted is He, returns man to the lowest of the low in creation, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And among you is he who is returned to the most decrepit age.﴾ [An-Nahl: 70]. Thus, whenever a person's age increases, he changes to something worse, whether in physical strength, physical form, freshness of face, or otherwise; he is returned to the lowest of the low.

And if we say that ﴿best of stature﴾ includes even the fitrah upon which Allah created creation, and the worship that follows from or is built upon this fitrah, then this is an indication that among people is one whose condition brings him back, and Allah forbid, to become the lowest of the low after having been at the highest and summit of faith and knowledge. The verse includes both meanings together.

And if we say that ﴿best of stature﴾ includes even the fitrah upon which Allah created creation, and the worship that follows from or is built upon this fitrah, then this is an indication that among people is one whose condition brings him back, and Allah forbid, to become the lowest of the low after having been at the highest and summit of faith and knowledge. The verse includes both meanings together.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Except for those who believe and do righteous deeds, for them is a reward never to be cut off.﴾ [al-Tin 6] This is an exception from His saying: ﴿Then We return him to the lowest of the low﴾. That is: except for the believers who have faith and do righteous deeds, for they are not returned to the lowest of the low, because they hold firmly to their faith and their deeds, so they remain upon them until they die.

His saying: ﴿for them is a reward﴾, meaning a recompense, ﴿never to be cut off﴾, meaning not discontinued, and also not reproached with (ghayr mamnun bihi). The word ﴿mamnun﴾ can carry the meaning of "cut off" (al-qat') and can carry the meaning of "bestowing favour upon" (al-minnah). So they have a reward that is not cut off and that is not bestowed upon them with reproach; that is, when they receive this reward they are not reminded of it by being told: "We gave you, and We did, and We did." And although the favour (minnah) belongs to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, upon them, through faith, righteous deeds and reward, all of it is a favour from Allah, yet it is not bestowed upon them in a reproachful manner; that is, they are not hurt by reproach as happens in worldly matters. If someone among people does you a kindness, he may often hurt you by reminding you of it: in every occasion he says, "I did this for you, I gave you," and similar things.

Then Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿So what causes you to deny the Judgment after this?﴾ [At-Tin 7]. Allah, exalted is He, shifted from speaking in the third person (ghaybah) to speaking in direct address and confrontation (khitab). He said: ﴿So what causes you to deny the Judgment after this?﴾, meaning: What is it that makes you deny, O mankind, after this clear evidence, ﴿the Judgment﴾, meaning: what Allah has commanded of religion (din). For this reason, whenever a person considers himself, his origin and his creation, and that Allah chose him and made his form good and his natural disposition (fitrah) good, he increases in faith in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and in affirming His Book and what His messengers have reported.

Then He said: ﴿Is not Allah the most just of judges?﴾ [At-Tin 8]. This interrogative is for affirmation: Allah, may He be exalted, affirms that He is the most just of judges. Here "ahkam" (most judicious/most just) is an elative (ism tafdil), and it is derived from al-hikmah (wisdom) and from al-hukm (judgment). The greatest and most supreme judgment, which nothing can oppose, is the judgment of Allah, may He be exalted, and the highest, most perfect wisdom is the wisdom of Allah, may He be exalted. So He, glorified and exalted, is the most judicious of judges in both His decree (qadar) and His legislation (shar'): to Him belongs judgment, and to Him all matters are returned.

We have been keen for the tafsir to be at the end of the parts of the Qur'an, because it is recited frequently in the prayers. And every believer ought to be keen to know the meanings of the Book of Allah, may He be exalted, for acting upon the Qur'an is not sound except by knowing its meaning. Indeed, Allah, exalted is He, described those who do not know its meaning as unlettered, saying: ﴿And among them are unlettered ones who do not know the Book except as wishful thinking﴾ [Al-Baqarah 78], meaning: except as mere recitation. Many people today, if I do not say most of them, know of the Qur'an nothing but the wording alone. It is fitting for students of knowledge that, whenever they gather with the common people, they bring a verse from the Book of Allah and explain it, especially those verses that are repeated often among the common people, such as al-Fatihah. If you were to bring a layman, indeed many people, and ask them about its meaning, they would not know anything of it.

We ask Allah, exalted is He, to grant us and you knowledge of His Book and the Sunnah of His Messenger (ﷺ), for He is capable of all things.
